section.title: Eliphaz's Second Speech
section.sectionRationale: The second cycle of speeches begins, and Eliphaz has lost the gentleness of his first address. He now accuses Job of undermining the fear of God, appeals again to the wisdom of elders, and paints an extended, almost gleeful picture of the wicked man's inevitable terror and ruin, a portrait he clearly intends Job to recognize himself in.
section.thesis: Eliphaz's second speech sharpens his earlier principle into open accusation, charging Job with arrogance and irreverence, and devotes most of its length to a vivid description of the wicked man's collapse that functions as a thinly veiled portrait of what Eliphaz now believes Job to be.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Eliphaz's rebuke that Job's words are empty and undermine the fear of God; his challenge asking whether Job was present at creation or has access to secrets no one else has; his extended, foreboding description of the wicked man's terror and inescapable fear; and his closing portrait of the wicked man's total ruin, stretched out against God and doomed to barrenness.

units.label: You undermine the fear of God

verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied:
"Does a wise man answer with empty counsel or fill his belly with the hot {{qadim|east wind}}?
Should he argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose?
But you even undermine the fear of God and hinder meditation before Him.
For your iniquity instructs your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty.
Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you.

units.label: Were you the first man ever born?
units.note: if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes

verses.text: "Were you the first man ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills?
Do you listen in on the {{sod|council}} of God or limit wisdom to yourself?
What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?
Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side, men much older than your father.
Are the consolations of God not enough for you, even words spoken gently to you?
Why has your heart carried you away, and why do your eyes flash,
as you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?
What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?
If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes,
how much less man, who is vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water?

units.label: The wicked man writhes in pain
units.note: he knows the day of darkness is at hand

verses.text: "Listen to me and I will inform you. I will describe what I have seen,
what was declared by wise men and was not concealed from their fathers,
to whom alone the land was given when no foreigner passed among them.
A {{rasha|wicked}} man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless.
Sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him.
He despairs of his return from darkness; he is marked for the sword.
He wanders about as food for vultures; he knows the day of darkness is at hand.
Distress and anguish terrify him, overwhelming him like a king poised to attack.

units.label: He stretched out his hand against God
units.note: their womb is pregnant with deceit

verses.text: "For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty,
rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield.
Though his face is covered with fat and his waistline bulges with flesh,
he will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.
He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure. His possessions will not overspread the land.
He will not escape from the darkness; the flame will wither his shoots, and the breath of God's mouth will carry him away.
Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward.
It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not flourish.
He will be like a vine stripped of its unripe grapes, like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.
For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery.
They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with {{mirmah|deceit}}."

qadim.gloss: The east wind, a hot, destructive desert wind in the ancient Near East, often associated in Scripture with judgment and withering. Eliphaz accuses Job of filling his belly with such wind, empty, damaging speech rather than substance.

sod.gloss: A council, intimate circle, or secret counsel. Eliphaz mockingly asks whether Job has listened in on God's own council, the same word used positively elsewhere of the LORD's confiding His counsel with those who fear Him, Psalm 25:14, turned here into an accusation of presumption.

rasha.gloss: The wicked, guilty, or condemned one, a central category in wisdom literature contrasted with the righteous, tsaddiq. Eliphaz's extended portrait of the rasha's inevitable terror and collapse functions as a barely disguised warning to Job, implying he now belongs to this category.

mirmah.gloss: Deceit, treachery, fraud. Eliphaz closes his speech by describing the wicked as a womb pregnant with mirmah, a vivid image of evil conceived and inevitably born, meant to warn Job of the fruit his own supposed inner corruption must eventually yield.

basic.context: Eliphaz speaks again, now more sharply than in his first address, accusing Job of undermining reverence for God with empty words drawn from his own iniquity. He challenges Job's presumption, asking whether he was present at creation or has secret access to God's council that other, wiser and older men lack. He then devotes most of his speech to an extended, almost relished description of the wicked man's inevitable terror, poverty, and ruin, an image clearly meant to warn Job that this fate awaits him unless he repents.
basic.hermeneutics: This speech shows the friends' theology hardening from gentle suggestion into direct accusation across the second cycle. Eliphaz's description of the wicked contains real and vivid poetic power, and portions of it echo true patterns Scripture elsewhere affirms about persistent, unrepentant wickedness; the error, again, is the specific and unevidenced application to Job, whom the reader knows to be innocent of the sins this portrait implies.
basic.originalLanguages: Eliphaz accuses Job of filling his belly with qadim, the hot east wind, empty and destructive speech, and mocks him for claiming access to God's sod, council, that wiser men lack. His extended portrait of the rasha, the wicked man, closes with the image of a womb pregnant with mirmah, deceit, evil conceived and inevitably born, aimed pointedly at Job though never naming him outright.
basic.typology: Eliphaz's insistence that no one, not even the heavens, is pure in God's eyes rightly anticipates the full biblical doctrine of universal sinfulness, though his application of it to explain Job's specific suffering remains mistaken; the tension between a true general doctrine and its wrongful specific application recurs throughout this cycle of speeches.
basic.christ: Eliphaz's claim that even the heavens are not pure in God's eyes, and how much less man, rightly anticipates Paul's later verdict that none is righteous, answered fully only in Christ, whose righteousness is given to sinners rather than achieved by them. Where Eliphaz uses universal sinfulness to accuse a specific innocent sufferer, the gospel uses the same universal truth to invite every sinner to the same free mercy, without requiring them to first prove which specific sin caused their present trouble.
basic.god: God is portrayed as a searching, exacting judge before whom even angels and heavens fall short, a true picture as far as it goes. But the picture becomes distorted when Eliphaz assumes this exacting God must presently be punishing Job for some particular, locatable fault, rather than allowing that God's dealings with the righteous can include suffering with no such explanation.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:10-12 affirms no one is righteous, none who does good, echoing Eliphaz's claim about universal impurity; Psalm 25:14 speaks of the LORD's council, sod, shared with those who fear Him, a positive use of the same word Eliphaz uses accusingly; Proverbs 16:18 warns that pride precedes destruction, a theme underlying Eliphaz's portrait of the wicked man's downfall.
basic.oneStory: Eliphaz's second speech hardens true doctrine into a weaponized accusation against an innocent man, showing how quickly right theology can curdle into cruelty when detached from actual knowledge of a person's situation. His true insistence on universal human impurity finds its truly gracious answer not in accusation but in the righteousness freely given in Christ.

context.literary:
Job 15 opens the second round of the debate, and its shape is easy to trace. Verses 2 to 6 are a charge, verses 7 to 16 are a run of questions that press Job's claim to wisdom until it looks absurd, and verses 17 to 35 are one long poem on the fate of the wicked, introduced by a formal call to listen and a claim to be passing on what was seen. Eliphaz plays two roles in turn, prosecutor and teacher, and the poem is where the teacher takes over.

The speech is held together by a body image. In verse 2 Job is said to fill his belly with the east wind; in verse 35 the wicked are those whose belly, the same Hebrew noun, is pregnant with deceit. Job's words are wind, and the end of the wicked is a womb that produces only trouble. Between those two ends the speech moves from talk to consequences: what you say now, Eliphaz insists, is what you will reap.

The poem itself has a clear rhythm. Verses 20 to 24 describe the inner life of the wicked man, terror in his ears, darkness in his expectation. Verses 25 to 27 give the reason with a heavy word for "for", the reach of his hand against God. Verses 28 to 35 turn to the outer wreck: ruined cities, vanishing wealth, a withered vine, a burnt tent. Nothing in the poem is addressed to Job by name, and that is the point of its cruelty. It is a description that leaves the listener to draw the line.

Notice also how many of Eliphaz's questions are ones God will ask Job at the end of the book. "Were you brought forth before the hills?" and the picture of listening in on God's council anticipate the whirlwind, Job 38:4. Eliphaz asks them as an argument from strength; God will ask them as an invitation to worship.
context.historical:
Eliphaz is a Temanite, and Teman was a district of Edom, south east of the Dead Sea. The Prophets remember it for its wisdom: "Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?" Jeremiah 49:7, and Obadiah 8 speaks of the wise men of Edom. When Eliphaz claims the backing of ancestral teaching he speaks as a man from a place that prided itself on exactly that.

The appeal in verses 17 to 19 is worth hearing as his first audience would. Wisdom belonged to the elders, the gray-haired, and it was handed down as something seen and tested rather than argued from scratch. Eliphaz adds that the land was given to those fathers "when no foreigner passed among them", an unusual boast that presents his tradition as uncontaminated by outside voices. It is a claim to purity of transmission, and it is offered against a man whose own experience seems to contradict the tradition.

The images belong to a world of herds, tents and desert edges. The east wind, qadim, is the scorching wind off the desert that thinned the ears of grain in Pharaoh's dream, Genesis 41:6, and dried up the fruit of a vine, Ezekiel 19:12. The "thick, studded shield" is a war shield whose bosses take the impact of a charge. The "tents of bribery" belong to the setting of village justice, where a payment to a judge could tilt a case.

Several details land uncomfortably close to what the reader knows of Job's own losses. The destroyer who attacks in prosperity, verse 21, the fire that consumes a tent, verse 34, and wealth that does not last, verse 29, echo the raiders and the fire of God in Job 1:13 to 19. Eliphaz means them as evidence against Job. The reader sees that he is quoting the plot of a story whose cause he cannot see.
context.canonical:
The chief line of the speech, "What is man, that he should be pure", picks up Eliphaz's own vision in Job 4:17 to 19 and is echoed by Bildad in Job 25:4 to 6. Outside the book the same conviction is stated as true doctrine: "no one alive is righteous before You", Psalm 143:2, and "there is no one who does good, not even one", Psalm 14:3, which Paul gathers into his case against every mouth in Romans 3:10 to 12. The teaching is sound. It is Eliphaz's use of it that is not.

His picture of the wicked has many parallels in the wisdom books. The lamp that goes out, the tree that does not flourish, and the tent that is destroyed all appear in Proverbs, and in the Psalms the wicked are swept away by terrors, Psalm 73:19. The image of conceiving trouble and giving birth to evil in verse 35 is shared with Psalm 7:14 and Isaiah 59:4, and James uses the same birth picture for sin's path from desire to death, James 1:15.

Eliphaz's confident tone is itself a canonical warning. Paul quotes his first speech, "He catches the wise in their craftiness", as Scripture, 1 Corinthians 3:19, using Job 5:13. The line is true, yet the book as a whole tells us Eliphaz applied truths like it wrongly. The final verdict is spoken by God: "you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has", Job 42:7. That leaves a lasting lesson for how to read the friends: their sentences can be true, and their speeches can still be wrong about the person in front of them, and Scripture records them without endorsing their verdicts.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer of Job gives Eliphaz a long and forceful speech because he wants the reader to feel the pull of the friends' case at its strongest. This speech has ancestral authority, poetic power and a large measure of doctrinal truth. A reader who is not careful will be persuaded. The book wants us to be moved by it and then to notice, from what we know of chapters 1 and 2, what it leaves out.

The speech also shows how a conversation about God goes wrong. Eliphaz begins by treating Job's honest questions as a threat to reverence, and he ends by treating a general truth about the wicked as a private verdict on one man. The writer means his hearers to learn to tell the difference between a doctrine and a diagnosis.

There is a warning for the teacher here as well. Eliphaz speaks of the "consolations of God" and of gentle words, verse 11, yet what Job has heard from him is an accusation. The writer invites everyone who counsels the suffering to ask what their words sound like from the other side of the ash heap.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Eliphaz said. It does not prescribe it. Scripture preserves the friends' speeches, and God's verdict in Job 42:7 tells us that their claims about God were not accurate. So when Eliphaz says the wicked man suffers all his days, verse 20, we should not lift it out as a promise or a rule of thumb about every hardship.

What can be taken as sound is narrower: that persistent defiance of God ends in ruin, and that no one stands pure before Him. Other texts affirm both. What cannot be taken from the chapter is the move from those truths to the conclusion that anyone who suffers is being punished for hidden wickedness.

The practical application is pastoral. Do not use a true general doctrine to explain another person's particular pain. Job's own book, and Jesus' answer about the man born blind and the tower that fell, Luke 13:4 to 5, both refuse that inference. The better instinct is the one the friends showed for seven days, sitting with the sufferer before explaining anything, Job 2:13.

debates.question: Is Eliphaz's portrait of the wicked man true?

views.label: True in general, wrongly applied
views.case: Much of the imagery matches the rest of Scripture. The wicked are pursued by terror, their wealth does not endure, and their house is finally consumed, as the Psalms and Proverbs say. On this reading the fault is not the portrait but the aim: it is pointed at Job, who is blameless by God's own testimony, Job 1:8.

views.label: Mistaken as a law of life
views.case: Job himself will argue that the wicked often prosper and die in comfort, Job 21:7 to 13. On this view, Eliphaz turns a tendency into a rule, and the speech is wrong about how the world works, not only about Job. God's rebuke at the end includes all three friends, Job 42:7.

views.label: A deliberate half truth
views.case: Some see the poem as carefully built to be almost right, so that the reader has to weigh each line rather than dismiss the whole speech. Its power lies in how much of it is recognisable.

debates.bearing: Whichever weight you give each view, the same discipline follows. Read the speech as a sample of persuasive religious talk that is partly true, test each line against the rest of Scripture, and refuse the step from 'the wicked suffer' to 'the sufferer is wicked'.

debates.question: Does Job undermine the fear of God, as Eliphaz says in verse 4?

views.label: Yes, his complaints are irreverent
views.case: Eliphaz hears Job's accusations, that God has become his enemy, as speech that erodes reverence. A tradition that values quiet submission will find some sympathy here.

views.label: No, his complaints are a form of faith
views.case: Job never leaves God. He says, 'Though He slay me, I will hope in Him', Job 13:15, and keeps appealing to God against God. God later says Job spoke of Him accurately, Job 42:7, which cannot be said of Eliphaz.

views.label: Both are partly right about their own concern
views.case: Job's language is at times extreme, and God's answer in chapters 38 to 41 corrects it. But the correction is not the one Eliphaz wants. God corrects Job's ignorance, not his honesty.

debates.bearing: The fear of God is not the absence of hard questions. The book counts honest lament directed at God as closer to faith than tidy speeches about God offered to a friend.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the word behind "crafty" in verse 5. The Hebrew arum, plural arumim, is the same word used of the serpent in Genesis 3:1, and Job 5:12 uses it of the plans of the crafty that God thwarts. It can be neutral, even positive, as "prudent" in Proverbs. Eliphaz uses it in the harsh sense, saying that Job's guilt is what trains his tongue, so that a sincere man is recast as a slippery one.

In verse 4 Job is said to hinder "meditation" before God. The noun here, sicha, comes from the same root as the word behind Job's own "complaint" in Job 7:13. That is a telling overlap. What Eliphaz calls hindered devotion is the same speech that Job calls his complaint, and the book does not let us assume that the two are opposites.

Verse 13, one more note on breath, says Job turns his "spirit" against God. The word is ruach, breath or wind, the same word family as the "east wind" of verse 2 and the "breath" of God's mouth that carries the wicked away in verse 30. The chapter plays on that word: Job's ruach, empty wind, against God's ruach, which is the real force. Eliphaz used the same picture in Job 4:9.

In verses 15 and 16 the "holy ones" are a category, probably heavenly beings, mentioned also in Job 5:1 and 4:18, whom God does not fully trust. Then comes an argument from lesser to greater with the phrase "how much less", the same pattern as Job 4:19. The verse ends with a striking simile: the wicked man "drinks injustice like water". Wrongdoing is not an occasional act but a thirst.

Verse 31 tells Job not to trust in "emptiness", shav, a word for what is worthless or false, used in the commandment about taking God's name "in vain", Exodus 20:7. Eliphaz says the reward for such trust is the same thing, so that the judgment matches the hope exactly.

The Hebrew of verse 15 and 16 also carries a moral weight in the little word "trust": God puts no trust in His holy ones, using the verb of firm reliance that Job 4:18 uses too, so the charge is about reliability under testing, not about physical make up.

Finally, verse 35 gathers three terms into a chain of birth, conceive, give birth, and prepare in the belly. It is a compact picture of evil moving from desire to deed, and it is close to what James later says about sin, James 1:15.

typology.type: The 'holy ones' and the heavens that are not pure, verses 15 to 16
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz argues that if even the heavens are unclean in God's eyes, man cannot claim purity. The idea of a standard that no creature meets on its own prepares for the New Testament teaching that righteousness must be given, not achieved, Romans 3:22 to 24. The correspondence is real, but the type falls short. Eliphaz has no answer to the problem he names, so he uses it as a hammer. In Christ the same truth becomes the reason for grace, since He is the one 'holy, innocent, undefiled', Hebrews 7:26, who gives purity to those who could never reach it.

typology.type: The wicked man's scorched vine and shed blossom, verses 30 to 33
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a plant that never bears, its shoots withered and its blossoms lost, recalls the language of Israel as a vine and of fruit as the test of a life, Isaiah 5:1 to 7. Jesus takes up the image of the vine and says of Himself, 'I am the true vine', John 15:1. The escalation is that fruit comes from remaining in Him, not from the vine's own strength. The type breaks at Eliphaz's assumption: the true Vine was pruned and cut off in death without any fault of His own, and bore fruit by that very cutting, John 12:24.

typology.type: Job as the one accused by those who claim to speak for God
typology.fulfillment: Job is charged with wickedness by respectable teachers on the strength of his suffering. The pattern reaches its height in the servant who was 'stricken by God' in the eyes of onlookers, Isaiah 53:4, and in Jesus, who was condemned by religious leaders who believed they were defending God, Mark 14:63 to 64. The correspondence is a pattern of innocent suffering misread as guilt. It falls short in one place: Job was not sinless, and his suffering did not bear anyone else's sin, while Christ's did, 1 Peter 2:22 to 24.

study.christ:
This speech leads to Christ most clearly by the problem it names and the way it misuses it. Eliphaz says that the heavens are not pure in God's eyes and that man is vile and corrupt, verses 14 to 16. The gospel does not argue with that. It agrees, and then it answers it: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God', 2 Corinthians 5:21. What Eliphaz uses to close a door the gospel uses to open one.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the question of who has stood in the counsel of God. Eliphaz taunts Job, 'Do you listen in on the council of God?', verse 8. The Old Testament sets a real answer beside that question. The counsel of the LORD is shared with the reverent, Psalm 25:14, and the false prophets are those who never stood in it, Jeremiah 23:18. John says of the Son that He is 'at the Father's side' and has made God known, John 1:18, and Jesus says He speaks what He has heard from the Father, John 8:26. What Eliphaz treats as an absurd claim is the ordinary position of the Son.

It leads to Christ by pattern in the way an innocent man is condemned by his words. Eliphaz says, 'Your own mouth condemns you', verse 6. The council said something similar of Jesus: 'Why do we need any more witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy', Mark 14:63. In both scenes religious authority reads a sufferer's words as proof of guilt. Jesus, unlike Job, was without sin, and His silence, Isaiah 53:7, is the opposite of the outpouring of Job, yet the shape of the injustice is the same.

The picture of the wicked man rushing at God with a thick shield, verses 25 to 26, has a gospel counterpart. At Gethsemane, the crowds came out with swords and clubs against one who did not resist, Matthew 26:47 and 52. The armed aggression of the wicked in Eliphaz's poem meets its worst example in the arrest of the one man who never lifted his hand against God.

The chapter should not be pressed into a code where every image is a portrait of Jesus. The links here rest on the New Testament's own use of the ideas of purity, counsel, and unjust condemnation. What Job 15 provides is a shadow of the problem, a man judged by those who think they speak for God, and the gospel provides the person who bears the true verdict in his place.
study.god:
The God Eliphaz describes is holy, and that is true. He is a God before whom nothing created is finally pure, verses 15 and 16, and this teaching stands. Isaiah's vision of the seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy', Isaiah 6:3, and his cry of undoneness, Isaiah 6:5, come from the same conviction. The chapter reminds a reader that reverence is not optional and that God's holiness is not a matter of degree.

The chapter also holds a picture of God as one who judges the arrogant. The wicked man stretches out his hand against God and rushes at Him with a shield, verses 25 and 26, and the breath of God's mouth carries him away, verse 30. It is a God who cannot be attacked with impunity. The prophets and psalms say the same, and they do so without hesitating over the justice of it.

Where the doctrine goes wrong is where it turns God into a machine that returns suffering for sin in exact measure. Eliphaz needs God to be predictable, since only a predictable God lets him name the cause of Job's grief. The book will not permit that. God's wisdom in chapters 38 to 41 is not a wisdom of tidy accounts but of a creator whose ways exceed his creature's understanding, and God Himself calls Job His servant while Job is still on the ash heap, Job 42:8.

There is a tension here worth holding rather than resolving. God is just, and the wicked do come to ruin. God is also free, and He sometimes permits the righteous to suffer for reasons He does not share, as the first two chapters show. Verses 14 to 16 make the first point strongly, and Job 42:7 to 8 refuses the inference. The God of the Bible is not less than Eliphaz says; He is more.

For worship, the chapter gives two lessons. The first is to keep Eliphaz's awe: God is holy and cannot be manipulated. The second is to refuse his certainty. Worship that names God's ways exactly, and applies them to others, has stopped being worship and has become a system. The better prayer is the one that Job's friends never offered for him, and that God in the end told them to offer with him: a sacrifice and a request for mercy, Job 42:8.

crossReferences.note: Eliphaz's first speech gives the vision from which verses 14 to 16 are drawn: no mortal is purer than his Maker, and God charges even His angels with error. The second speech repeats the same argument with harder edges, showing how a private revelation has hardened into a public accusation.

Wisdom herself speaks of being brought forth before the hills, verse 25. Eliphaz's mocking question 'Were you brought forth before the hills?' echoes that language and treats wisdom as a matter of seniority, when Proverbs treats it as a gift from God who was there first.

God's first question from the whirlwind, 'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?', is the true form of Eliphaz's challenge. Eliphaz asks to shame Job; God asks to show him how small his sight is and how large God's care for the world remains.

The LORD confides in those who fear Him. The Psalm uses the same idea Eliphaz denies to Job, the sod or council of God, and gives it to the reverent, which shows that the accusation of verse 8 mocks something Scripture treats as a real privilege.

The false prophets are those who never stood in the council of the LORD. This is the test Eliphaz wants to apply to Job's speeches. The text turns it on Eliphaz's own confidence, since he claims to speak from a vision and from tradition, and God will say he did not speak rightly, Job 42:7.

Job's answer to this whole line of thought: the wicked live on, grow old and prosper. It is the direct reply to the claim that the wicked man 'writhes in pain all his days', verse 20, and it shows that Eliphaz has a doctrine of tendencies, not a law.

The wicked man 'conceives trouble and births falsehood', a picture that verse 35 shares almost word for word. The birth image explains why Eliphaz sees evil as inevitable: what is conceived will be delivered, and what is delivered will be paid for.

James uses the same picture of conception and birth for the path from desire to sin and from sin to death. It shows that the picture of verse 35 is fair as a description of how sin grows, which makes its use against Job as a person all the more striking.

Paul gathers verses like Psalm 14 into his case that no one is righteous. He agrees with the doctrine of verses 14 to 16, and then, unlike Eliphaz, moves at once to the righteousness of God given through faith, Romans 3:21 to 24.

The final word on the friends. God says they did not speak accurately about Him and sends them to Job for prayer. The judgment reaches back over the whole debate and tells the reader how to hear Eliphaz's careful and passionate case.

study.oneStory:
The book of Job asks a question that runs from Eden to the cross: why do the righteous suffer, and who speaks for God when they do? Eliphaz's second speech is one of the most forceful attempts in Scripture to answer it with a system. Its answer is that suffering is the wages of wickedness, and that anyone who resists that reading is only proving his guilt.

The Bible, taken whole, shows why that answer is both attractive and wrong. Since Genesis 3 the world is under a real curse, and the wicked do come to ruin, and the psalms and proverbs say so. But Genesis 4 shows Abel, a righteous man, killed by his brother, and the ordering of that chapter already breaks the simple equation. Job carries the tension to its sharpest point by placing a man whom God calls blameless under the worst of afflictions.

What Eliphaz cannot supply is a way for a sinner to stand before the holy God he describes, and a way for an innocent sufferer to be understood. The rest of Scripture builds toward both answers. The prophets speak of a servant who suffers without cause and is accounted guilty by others, Isaiah 53:3 to 5. The Psalms teach a people to bring complaint to God rather than about Him. And Christ comes as the truly blameless one who is condemned by the words of those who claim to know God's mind, and who takes the judgment described in this chapter on behalf of others.

That is why the chapter's true doctrine of human impurity does not end in despair for those in Christ. The 'holy ones' who are not pure in God's sight are answered by the multitude in white robes washed in the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 7:14. The tents of bribery, the barren company of the godless, and the fire that consumes give way to the city where nothing unclean will enter and where there is no more curse, Revelation 21:27 and 22:3.

In the meantime the chapter leaves believers with a warning and a task. The warning is against speaking for God with more confidence than we have earned. The task is the one God gave Job's friends at the end: to bring a sacrifice, and to ask the sufferer to pray for us, Job 42:8.

quiz.q: What accusation does Eliphaz make against Job in 15:4-6 that is sharper than his first speech?

options.text: That Job undermines the fear of God and that his own words condemn him, not Eliphaz's accusations.
options.note: This direct charge of irreverence marks an escalation from the gentler tone of Eliphaz's first speech in chapters 4 to 5.

options.text: That Job's own iniquity now instructs his mouth and shapes the crafty way he argues.
options.note: A close paraphrase of Eliphaz's actual charge in verse 5, though less direct than his explicit statement that Job's own words condemn him.

options.text: That Job has never actually suffered any real loss.
options.note: Eliphaz does not deny Job's suffering; his accusation concerns the content and attitude of Job's speech.

options.text: That Job has stolen from the poor.
options.note: No such specific charge of theft appears in this speech; the accusation concerns Job's irreverent speech, not a named crime.

quiz.q: What challenge does Eliphaz pose to Job in 15:7-10?

options.text: Whether Job was present at creation or has access to God's secret council that wiser, older men do not have.
options.note: Eliphaz mocks Job's presumption in claiming insight the collective wisdom of elders supposedly does not possess.

options.text: Whether Job knows something the gray-haired and aged among them do not already know.
options.note: Captures part of Eliphaz's challenge, though less complete than his fuller claim about creation and God's own council.

options.text: Whether Job's friends are older than he is.
options.note: Eliphaz does mention that older, wiser men agree with the friends' position, but his main challenge concerns Job's presumed access to divine secrets, not simple age comparison.

options.text: Whether Job has ever actually prayed to God.
options.note: The challenge concerns claimed special knowledge, not whether Job prays at all.

quiz.q: What does most of Eliphaz's second speech (15:17-35) describe?

options.text: An extended, vivid portrait of the wicked man's inevitable terror, poverty, and ruin.
options.note: This portrait occupies most of the chapter and is clearly intended as a veiled warning to Job.

options.text: A description of terrors, sudden calamity, and darkness overtaking someone who has vaunted himself against the Almighty.
options.note: True to the chapter's content, though less complete than recognizing this entire portrait as a warning aimed at Job.

options.text: A neutral historical account with no application to Job.
options.note: Though Job is never named directly in this portrait, its placement and rhetorical function clearly aim it at him.

options.text: A detailed defense of Job's innocence.
options.note: The chapter argues the opposite; Eliphaz's portrait implies Job belongs among the wicked he describes.

quiz.q: What true doctrine does Eliphaz correctly affirm in 15:14-16, even while misapplying his overall argument?

options.text: That no human being, and not even the heavens, is pure before God.
options.note: This claim of universal impurity before God is affirmed elsewhere in Scripture, such as Romans 3:10-12, even though Eliphaz misuses it to accuse Job specifically.

options.text: That man, who is vile and corrupt, drinks injustice like water.
options.note: A true, vivid restatement of the same underlying claim, though less precise than Eliphaz's fuller argument from the impurity of the heavens down to man.

options.text: That God's council is available to anyone who asks.
options.note: Eliphaz uses the idea of God's council, sod, to mock Job's presumed access to it, not to offer it broadly.

options.text: That some people are entirely without sin.
options.note: Eliphaz explicitly denies this, insisting no one, not even the heavens, is pure in God's eyes.

quiz.q: How should readers evaluate the mixture of true doctrine and false application in this chapter?

options.text: By recognizing that Eliphaz's general claims about human sinfulness are true, while his specific application of them to accuse Job is false, since the reader already knows Job's suffering was not caused by hidden sin.
options.note: This distinction between sound general doctrine and its unproven specific application is central to understanding all three friends' speeches.

options.text: By affirming the true doctrine Eliphaz states while questioning whether it actually explains Job's particular situation.
options.note: Captures the right approach in principle, though less precise than naming exactly what the reader already knows from chapters 1 and 2.

options.text: By concluding that everything Eliphaz says in this chapter must be rejected as false.
options.note: Some of Eliphaz's claims, such as universal human sinfulness, are affirmed elsewhere in Scripture as true; the error is specifically in his application to Job.

options.text: By concluding that Job must indeed be guilty as Eliphaz suggests.
options.note: The book's own frame in chapters 1 and 2 establishes that Job's suffering was not caused by sin, directly contradicting Eliphaz's application.

questions: Eliphaz's warnings about the wicked man's downfall are vivid, detailed, and aimed at someone he never actually names. Have you ever spoken indirectly about someone's supposed faults rather than addressing them honestly and directly?

Eliphaz correctly says no one is pure before God, yet uses that truth cruelly. What true things about human sinfulness do you know, and how do you make sure you use them to humble yourself rather than to judge others?

Eliphaz assumes that because Job disagrees with the collective wisdom of elders, he must be wrong. Where do you weigh popular or traditional opinion against your own honest reading of a situation, and how do you tell the difference between humility and mere conformity?

This speech shows theology hardening into accusation across repeated cycles of conflict. Have you noticed your own position toward someone hardening over the course of a disagreement, even when the underlying facts have not changed?

Eliphaz's true doctrine of universal sinfulness is meant by Scripture to lead to grace in Christ, not condemnation of a specific sufferer. Where do you need to receive that grace for yourself this week rather than turning true doctrine into self-accusation or the judgment of others?

translationNotes.note: The hot east wind, qadim, was a well-recognized destructive force in the ancient Near East, often linked to divine judgment elsewhere in Scripture, such as the wind that dries up Jonah's plant, Jonah 4:8.

Council renders sod, elsewhere used positively of the LORD's intimate counsel shared with those who fear Him, Psalm 25:14; Eliphaz here uses the same word mockingly to accuse Job of claiming an access he does not have.

Their womb is pregnant with deceit is a vivid metaphor of evil conceived internally and inevitably brought to birth, a common wisdom-literature image for how sin produces its own destructive consequences.
